property_summary: The owner() function must return the address that initially deployed the Ownable contract; the bug returns address(0) regardless of deployment, so for any deployment the correct owner is non-zero while the buggy owner is zero.
The owner() function must return the deployer of the outermost Ownable contract; the bug returns address(0) regardless of deployment.

The owner() getter must return the address that originally deployed the contract (the msg.sender of the Ownable constructor), which is never the zero address; the bug makes it always return address(0).
owner() must return the address that deployed the Ownable-derived contract; the mutant incorrectly returns address(0) for any caller.
The owner() function must return the address that was the original deployer of the Ownable contract, which is non-zero; the buggy version always returns address(0), breaking this rule.

The owner() function should return the stored owner address set during Ownable construction, not the current msg.sender, so calling owner() as a non-owner returns the same address regardless of who calls it; the mutant returns the caller instead, breaking the invariant that owner() is constant for a given contract.

For any caller, c.owner() must equal the address that deployed the Ownable contract (the initial msg.sender of Ownable's constructor), regardless of who calls it; the mutant breaks this by returning msg.sender, so a non-deployer caller gets a different value.

For any caller, c.owner() must return the same address as the stored _owner set during Ownable's construction. The mutant breaks this by returning msg.sender, so two different prank callers see different return values, which the correct contract cannot produce.

For every caller address, calling owner() returns the same constant address (the initial deployer of the Ownable contract), but the mutant makes it return the caller's address, so a non-deployer caller receives a different value.

For any two different callers, c.owner() returns the same address, because it always returns the stored _owner regardless of msg.sender; the mutant returns msg.sender, so two different callers get different results.
The owner() function must return the address that deployed the contract, not the contract's own address. The bug makes owner() return address(this) instead.
For any address that originally deployed the contract, calling owner() must return that deployer's address, not the contract's own address; the mutant returns address(this) instead.
The owner() function must return the address that originally deployed the contract, not the contract's own address; the mutant returns address(this) instead.
For any address that deploys C, the owner() view must return the deployer, not the contract's own address; the buggy version always returns address(this) instead.
Calling owner() must return the deployer of the contract (address(this) in setUp), while the mutant returns the contract's own address.

After a successful call to transferOwnership(newOwner), the owner() must equal newOwner; the mutant leaves the owner unchanged so owner() still returns the old owner, violating this invariant for any valid newOwner.
After calling transferOwnership with a non-zero address by the current owner, the owner() must return the new owner; the mutant leaves the owner unchanged.

After the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) with newOwner != address(0), reading c.owner() must return newOwner; the mutant emits the event but leaves the owner unchanged, so c.owner() stays the old owner.

After the current owner successfully calls transferOwnership to a non-zero newOwner, the old owner can no longer call onlyOwner functions successfully; the mutant's unchanged _owner lets the old owner still act, so a subsequent renounceOwnership() by the old owner succeeds on the mutant but fails on the reference.

After any call to transferOwnership(newOwner) where newOwner is not address(0), the previous owner can no longer execute onlyOwner functions; the bug leaves _owner unchanged so the old owner retains privileges.

The name() function must return a value that equals the constructor-supplied ERC20 name. The reference returns the storage-backed name, while the mutant returns a hardcoded string, so any deployment with a non-matching constructor argument will produce a mismatch.

The name() function must return a value that matches the _name storage variable set during construction; the buggy version always returns "DCF Token" regardless of the state-changing operations, causing a mismatch when the contract is not altered.

For any deployment, calling name() must return the ERC20 token name defined in the constructor. The reference returns the stored _name, while the mutant always returns the literal string "DCF Token" which equals the constructor argument in the default deployment but would differ if the contract were constructed with a different name string.

For any instance of C, a call to name() must return exactly the _name argument passed to the ERC20 constructor; the mutant breaks this by returning the hardcoded "DCF Token" which causes a mismatch when the constructor is called with any other string.

For any C deployed via new C(address(this)), a subsequent call to name() must return the _name argument passed to the ERC20 constructor; the mutant violates this by returning the hardcoded string "DCF Token" which equals the constructor argument in default deployment but would differ if constructed with a different name string.
The name() function for the correct contract returns the exact string passed to the ERC20 constructor ("DCF Token"), while the mutant always returns an empty string.
For any caller, the return value of c.name() is a non-empty string (specifically the token name), but the mutant returns an empty string.
For the immutable name set during construction, calling name() always returns the same fixed non-empty string, but the mutant returns the empty string.
For any call to name(), the return value must equal the constant token name 'DCF Token', while the mutant returns an empty string for all inputs.
Calling c.name() must return a non-empty string, but the mutant returns the empty string.

For any valid constructor argument, calling name() on the contract C returns exactly the string passed as the name_ parameter to ERC20's constructor. The buggy version returns the symbol string instead, violating this rule for any constructor argument where name and symbol differ.
